explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is. At Perga, John left them “to return to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:13). Why? The verse doesn't say, and I'm not about to make something up. So the crew is one man short, and everybody else keeps moving, friend.

Tarsus doesn't show up on this trip, friend. The verse says John left them at Perga “to return to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:13). So he heads back to Jerusalem while Paul and the others keep going. Don't worry about the map. I once got lost walking from my oven to my cookie box, and that's FOUR steps.

Joppa's not where this road goes, friend. John heads back to Jerusalem from Perga, and the others keep traveling without him (Acts 13:13). Hold on to that name John, because Paul is going to mention a different John later, and I don't want you mixing them up like I mix up my sprinkle jars.

That's right! In Pisidian Antioch, they “entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down” (Acts 13:14). After that long trip inland from Perga, I'd sit down too. Shoot, I'd sit down and ask for a pillow. But they're not just resting, friend. Sitting in that synagogue puts them right where the next thing happens.

It's true, friend. After the trip inland from Perga, they “entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down” (Acts 13:14). Think about it. You walk ALL that way, you find the synagogue, and you take a seat. That's exactly what they do, and that seat is about to turn into a pulpit.

Encouragement, friend! The synagogue leaders send word, “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak” (Acts 13:15). They read from the Law and the Prophets, then they open the floor to the visitors. That's an open mic, and Paul is about to take it.

Nope, no warning. The leaders ask for a word of encouragement (Acts 13:15). Friend, nobody walks up to a guest speaker and says, “Hey, could you scare us a little?” Not if they ever want a guest speaker again.

I get it. The Prophets were JUST read out loud, so that word was still hanging in the air (Acts 13:15). But what the leaders ask the visitors for is a word of encouragement, something for the people. And friend, Paul does NOT need to be asked twice. He's on his feet in the very next verse (Acts 13:16).

True! Paul says of God, “He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness” (Acts 13:18). Forty years, friend. I lose patience waiting forty SECONDS for my oven to preheat. God's patience with His people is a whole different level.

Oh, it's true. Forty YEARS of it out in the wilderness (Acts 13:18). And after all that, God still gives His people the land as an inheritance (Acts 13:19). Friend, I can't put up with my own humming for forty minutes.

A king, friend. Paul says, “Then the people asked for a king,” and God gave them Saul son of Kish (Acts 13:21). They've had judges, they've had Samuel the prophet, and now they want a crown on somebody. And God answers that request.

No construction project here. “Then the people asked for a king” (Acts 13:21), and God gave them Saul son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin. Paul's history goes from judges to crowns, not bricks. Which is a shame, friend, because I'd have volunteered to stamp every single brick.

Good guess, since Paul just name-dropped Samuel the prophet. But Samuel is where the judges end (Acts 13:20). What comes next is “Then the people asked for a king” (Acts 13:21). Judges, prophet, king. Friend, Paul is flying through Israel's history so fast I'd need a cookie timer just to keep up.

David, friend! After removing Saul, God “raised up David as their king” and called him “a man after My own heart” (Acts 13:22). And keep your eye on David, because Paul isn't done with him. He's about to connect David to the Savior.

Jonathan doesn't even get a mention in Paul's sermon. Paul goes straight from removing Saul to “He raised up David as their king” (Acts 13:22). No stops in between, friend. That's me going from the oven to the cookie box when the batch smells THAT good.

Samuel's the prophet, and Paul puts him at the end of the time of the judges (Acts 13:20). The crown goes to David (Acts 13:22). Samuel as king would be like me trying to be the cookie box, friend. Great at my job. Not THAT job.

Sandals! John says, “But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie” (Acts 13:25). Not worthy to untie them. That's humility, friend. I get a little proud when my sprinkles land straight. And the One John is pointing to is Jesus.

Lower, friend. All the way down to the feet. John says he's not worthy to untie the sandals of the One coming after him, and that One is Jesus (Acts 13:25). Belts, I can't help you with anyway. I don't wear one. My apron strings do all the work, and they are working HARD.

Look down, way down. It's the sandals John says he's not worthy to untie (Acts 13:25). He's pointing past himself to the One coming after him, and that's Jesus. Me, I point with my mustache, friend, and half the time I knock over a sprinkle jar doing it.

They came up empty, friend. No ground for a death sentence. Not a crumb of a reason. And they still went to Pilate, the governor of Judea (Luke 3:1), and asked him to have Jesus executed (Acts 13:28).

False is right. Paul says they “found no ground for a death sentence” (Acts 13:28). Let that sink in, friend. They had NOTHING on Him, and they still asked Pilate, the governor of Judea (Luke 3:1), to have Him executed (Acts 13:28).

That tomb was not His forever address, friend. Paul says it plain: “But God raised Him from the dead” (Acts 13:30). They laid Him in a tomb (Acts 13:29), and God raised Him. That's the turning point of Paul's whole sermon.

False! After they laid Him in a tomb (Acts 13:29), Paul says, “But God raised Him from the dead” (Acts 13:30). That “But God” is my favorite little phrase, friend. Everything was going one way, and then BUT GOD.

explanations.answer: Those who came with Him from Galilee
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Paul says He was seen “by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:31). And those people are “now His witnesses to our people” (Acts 13:31). They walked with Him, they saw Him alive again, and now they tell it.

explanations.answer: The rulers who condemned Him in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Not the rulers, friend. Paul says those rulers didn't even recognize Jesus (Acts 13:27). After God raised Him, He was seen “by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:31). The ones who walked with Him are the ones who saw Him, and now they're His witnesses.

explanations.answer: The synagogue leaders of Pisidian Antioch
explanations.explanation: These folks are hearing about it from Paul, friend, not seeing it themselves. Paul says Jesus was seen “by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:31). The leaders in Antioch are the ones who asked for a word of encouragement (Acts 13:15). And boy, are they getting one.

Jesus, friend! Paul says, “But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay” (Acts 13:37). David served, died and saw decay (Acts 13:36), so that Psalm about the Holy One can't be about David. It's about Jesus, the Savior God brought to Israel (Acts 13:23). That's Paul connecting the dots like a pro.

Paul's only got two names on the board here, and Samuel isn't one of them. David saw decay (Acts 13:36), but the One God raised from the dead did not, and that's Jesus (Acts 13:37). Picking Samuel here is like me grabbing the sprinkle jar when the recipe says chocolate chips, friend. Good jar. Wrong cookie.

explanations.answer: Saul son of Kish from Benjamin
explanations.explanation: Saul left this sermon back when God removed him (Acts 13:22), and Paul isn't bringing him back for an encore. The One who did not see decay is the One God raised from the dead (Acts 13:37), and God raised Jesus (Acts 13:30). Friend, I know a thing or two about getting slid to the back of the drawer and staying there.

Moses, friend! Paul says that through Jesus “everyone who believes is justified from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses” (Acts 13:39). Everything, friend. EVERYTHING. What the law couldn't do for them, Jesus does for everyone who believes.

Abraham's in the sermon, but not in this line, friend. Paul calls them “children of Abraham” (Acts 13:26), but the law he names is the law of Moses (Acts 13:39). Through Jesus, everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses couldn't justify them from. That's the good news Paul is preaching.

David gets a LOT of airtime in this sermon, so I see why you went there, friend. But the law Paul names is “the law of Moses” (Acts 13:39). Through Jesus, everyone who believes is justified from everything that law couldn't justify them from. David's the king, Moses is the law.

Scoffers it is. Paul quotes the prophets: “Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish!” (Acts 13:41). Then the kicker: a work done in their days that they would never believe, even if someone told them (Acts 13:41). And Paul's last word to his listeners? Watch out that this doesn't happen to you (Acts 13:40). Friend, that's how you end a sermon.

No idols in this warning. The prophets' words Paul quotes call out scoffers (Acts 13:41), people who'd hear about a work done in their own days and still refuse to believe it. Friend, I'd make a terrible scoffer anyway. Tell me ANYTHING about cookies and I believe it on the spot.

It's the scoffers, friend. Paul quotes, “Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish!” (Acts 13:41). These are folks who wouldn't believe a work done in their own days, even if someone told them (Acts 13:41). That's me with a new cookie recipe. “That'll never work.” Then it works, and I look silly.

explanations.answer: Continue this message on the next Sabbath
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. The people urged them “to continue this message on the next Sabbath” (Acts 13:42). They want MORE. Paul just preached a whole sermon, and they're already asking for another one next week. That's the best review a preacher can get.

explanations.answer: Leave the city before the next Sabbath
explanations.explanation: The opposite, friend! The people urged them “to continue this message on the next Sabbath” (Acts 13:42). They aren't showing Paul and Barnabas the door. They're asking for a part two.

explanations.answer: Write this message down for the leaders
explanations.explanation: They want to HEAR it again, friend. The people urged them “to continue this message on the next Sabbath” (Acts 13:42). Nobody asks for a written copy. They want Paul back in person next week, and that's a sign the message landed.

Grace, friend! After the synagogue let out, many of the Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas, and the word they got was to “continue in the grace of God” (Acts 13:43). Keep going in it. Stay right there. That's me next to a fresh tray: as close as possible, for as long as possible.

Smart guess, since the law of Moses came up just a few verses back (Acts 13:39). But the send-off word is grace. Paul and Barnabas urge their followers to keep on in God's grace (Acts 13:43). Paul packs so much into one sermon, friend, I'd need to take notes. On a cookie. In chocolate chips.

No house keys being handed out here, friend. Paul and Barnabas urge the people following them “to continue in the grace of God” (Acts 13:43). Grace isn't an address. If it were, I'd have moved in already and parked my oven by the front door.

Jealousy, friend. When the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 13:45). Nearly the whole city shows up, and instead of joy, it's jealousy. Remember, I can't get three bakers to a taste test. If nearly the whole city lined up for somebody else's cookies, I'd smile real big. Through clenched teeth. Okay, I might need a minute.

Funny, “wonder” was in Paul's warning about scoffers (Acts 13:41). But here, when the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 13:45). And it doesn't stay quiet, friend. They start contradicting what Paul is saying.

It's jealousy, friend. When the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 13:45). Nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord (Acts 13:44). Not everyone is happy about that, and it shows.
The Gentiles! Paul and Barnabas say, “we now turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). They spoke the word to the Jews first, like they said they had to. Now the door swings wide open, friend. WIDE open.

Jerusalem's not on the itinerary. Since those Jews in Antioch reject the word, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). That's a turn, friend, not a U-turn. Me, I make about forty U-turns a day between the oven and the cookie box.
Paul and Barnabas aren't naming a town at all. They're naming a whole people: “we now turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Think bigger, friend. MUCH bigger. I get excited when I fill ONE cookie box.

The ends of the earth! The Lord's words go, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47). Friend, I've got one little cookie planet, and I still lose things on it. The Lord's talking about the whole EARTH, all the way to the edges.

Close, friend, but the word is ends. The Lord says, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47). Same big idea: salvation going as far as the earth goes. Paul and Barnabas say this is what the Lord commanded them.

The word is ends, friend. The Lord says, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47). The Gentiles are already named in the first half. The second half sends salvation as far as the earth goes.

explanations.answer: They celebrate and praise the Lord's message
explanations.explanation: Party in Pisidian Antioch! When the Gentiles heard this, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord” (Acts 13:48). They just heard the door is open for them, friend. You'd better believe they're celebrating.

explanations.answer: They hesitate and ask for a sign first
explanations.explanation: No hesitating here, friend. When the Gentiles heard this, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord” (Acts 13:48). They don't ask for a sign. They hear the message and they CELEBRATE.

explanations.answer: They go quiet and wait for their leaders
explanations.explanation: Quiet? Not even close, friend. When the Gentiles heard this, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord” (Acts 13:48). Nobody's waiting around for permission. They're rejoicing right then and there.

It gets out, friend! The verse says, “And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region” (Acts 13:49). Not just the city. The whole region. Kind of like when I sneak one cookie and somehow the whole bakery knows before the next batch is out.
False! “And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region” (Acts 13:49). One synagogue sermon, then nearly the whole city, and now the whole region. Friend, that message is MOVING.

explanations.answer: They are driven out of the district
explanations.explanation: Driven out, friend. They “stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district” (Acts 13:50). One Sabbath nearly the whole city shows up, and then they get pushed out of the district. But hold on, because they're not done.

explanations.answer: They are locked in the city jail
explanations.explanation: No jail cell in this one. Nobody locks them in. They get pushed OUT of the district (Acts 13:50). Friend, I know a little about getting pushed aside. I got slid behind the takeout menus. At least Paul and Barnabas got a whole open road.

explanations.answer: They are sent back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nobody ships them back to Jerusalem. The persecution gets stirred up, and they're driven out of the district, period (Acts 13:50). No escort, no return ticket. Friend, if somebody pushed me that hard, I'd roll right off my little planet.

Iconium! They “shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium” (Acts 13:51). Driven out of one district, and they just keep walking. Friend, if somebody chased me out of my bakery, I'd need a nap and a whole box of cookies. These two shake it off and head for the NEXT town.
Not Ephesus. They shake the dust off their feet and go to Iconium (Acts 13:51). Shake, stomp, walk. I tried shaking the dust off my feet once, friend, and I flung sprinkles across the entire bakery.

Corinth's not the stop. Iconium is (Acts 13:51). Look how they leave: they shake the dust off their feet in protest against them, and they go. When I get upset, friend, I don't shake anything off. I sulk. LOUDLY. Into a cookie box.
